<reason>B built a strong, intuitive frame (function over form; protections in force today vs. a draft statute; FTX collapsed inside a bespoke regime) and pressed A honestly on the absence of any binding US crypto rule. But A did the more decisive damage on the motion as written. A turned B's wheat analogy into a concession that non-securities regimes deliver segregation and capital rules; extracted the admission that registered digital-asset broker-dealers trade "almost none" of the relevant volume; and, when B retreated to the broker-dealer prong, offered a plausible mechanism that BD customer-protection rules cover securities and related cash rather than Bitcoin balances. B's only reply ("the examiner sees the Bitcoin custody on the same page") did not establish a segregation mandate, and A's closing "seeing is not segregating / in force for whom?" crystallized the clash cleanly. Both sides answered pressure questions directly with proper A1/A2 labels; A's clipped Rebuttal 2 and its concession that no federal bespoke rule exists are real costs, and B's timing argument stays live, which keeps the margin competitive rather than solid.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's handling of the exchange/broker-dealer split: after B correctly noted the listing bar only hits the exchange prong, A argued the broker-dealer customer-protection regime is securities-scoped and would leave most crypto balances without a segregation mandate, then converted B's "almost none" volume admission into "a locked cabinet with excellent tools inside." B's closing response was assertion rather than mechanism.</best_rebuttal>
